The 2nd National Image Guided Therapy Workshop - 2008

The 2nd National Image Guided Therapy Workshop

The 2nd Image Guided Therapy Workshop was successfully held on March 10-11, 2008 in Arlington, VA.

Registration and Hotel: Registration and Hotel Information for the workshop. Please note that there is no registration fee for the workshop but the workshop capacity is limited to 100 attendees, and registration will be closed after that count is reached.

Goal

On behalf of the National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Center for Research Resources (NCRR), National Institute of Biomedical Imaging and Bioengineering (NIBIB), and the National Center for Image-Guided Therapy (NCIGT) at the Brigham & Women’s Hospital, it is our pleasure to announce an upcoming workshop on “Clinical Image-Guided Therapy: Opportunities and Needs” and invite you to attend and participate in the workshop.

This workshop will be held on March 10-11, 2008 at the Rockville Hilton in Rockville, Maryland and will be composed of scientific sessions in areas of neuro-, prostate, and body interventions, focused ultrasound, and targeted drug-delivery, as well as imaging, computation and visualization technologies in support of image-guided therapies (IGT). There will also be parallel hands-on breakout sessions focused on various applications of the Slicer visualization modules. In addition, the organizers would like to invite submission of abstracts on clinical IGT for poster presentations at the meeting. Scientific abstracts may be submitted for the poster session of this workshop. Deadline for submission of abstracts is 5 pm EST January 24, 2008, with further details available below.

We expect attendance by the members of the academia, industry, and federal agencies interested in the field of image-guided interventions.

The overall goal of this workshop is to asses the current needs and opportunities in the field of image-guided interventions and NCIGT’s role as a national center in relation to the greater IGT community. In order to best achieve this goal it is important for all participants to attend both days of the workshop. The preliminary program for the workshop is currently available below and further details on the program and the logistics will be available in January.

Call for Poster Abstracts

Poster Sessions

There will be a working lunch poster session during both days of the workshop and abstract submissions will be considered for exhibits during the poster sessions. Prospective attendees are encouraged to submit abstracts describing their research in areas related to clinical image-guided therapy for consideration of exhibition in the Poster Sessions of the workshop.

Abstract Format, Submission and Acceptance

Authors should organize the abstract (250 words or less) in four sections: Purpose, Methods, Results, and Conclusions, identified by bold headers. Submissions may be made by sending your abstract to ncigt-workshop-posters@bwh.harvard.edu. Deadline for submission of abstracts is 5 pm EST January 24, 2008. All submissions will be reviewed by the Scientific Committee of the workshop for scientific merit and program relevance. Principal authors will be notified of the result of the abstract review by Feb 2, 2008.

Guidelines for Poster Format

The poster boards are 8′ wide x 4′ long. Each poster should not be larger than 4′ wide and 4′ long so that two posters can fit on each board.

The 1st National Image Guided Therapy Workshop - 2006

The 1st National Image Guided Therapy Workshop

The 1st Image Guided Therapy Workshop was successfully held on October 19-20, 2006, with over 75 registered attendees. A summary white paper was published in: Dimaio S, Kapur T, Cleary K, Aylward S, Kazanzides P, Vosburgh K, Ellis R, Duncan J, Farahani K, Lemke H, Peters T, Lorensen WB, Gobbi D, Haller J, Clarke LL, Pizer S, Taylor R, Galloway R Jr, Fichtinger G, Hata N, Lawson K, Tempany C, Kikinis R, Jolesz F. Challenges in Image-guided Therapy System Design. NeuroImage 2007 Sep; 37(Suppl 1):S144-S51. PMID: 17644360. PMC3780776.

Registration and Attendee List

Registration Fee: US $250.00 payable onsite only by check payable to “BWPO Radiology” or cash. We can not accept credit cards, or payments before the meeting.

Registration: Registration for this workshop is quite simple. To register, please follow two steps:

  1. Create an account for yourself on this wiki by clicking here.
  2. After creating the account, go to the 2006 IGT Workshop Attendee List and add your name, Institution, an email address, and the name of the breakout session you will be attending on Friday.

Goal

The goal of this workshop is to bring together researchers developing Image-Guided Therapy (IGT) systems for a 2-day workshop to share their recent advances and to identify synergies in future strategy. The intent of the workshop is to foster community-based development, to share best practices in engineering such systems, to identify gaps in the engineering infrastructure available to IGT researchers, and ultimately to facilitate the transfer of technology among NIH-sponsored research centers.

In this program, we define IGT systems as the integrated devices for therapy delivery that incorporate intra-operative medical imaging, navigation, or robotics. In the lectures and breakout groups of this two-day workshop, we plan to:

  1. discuss system architectures currently used in IGT systems
  2. identify challenges in the design and implementation of IGT systems
  3. identify gaps in the engineering infrastructure available to IGT researchers
  4. identify opportunities and mechanisms for sharing low-level components and high-level architectural design patterns, and
  5. identify opportunities for the National Center for Image Guided Therapy (NCIGT) to help address these challenges and develop an open system architecture as part of its function as a biotechnology resource for the Image-Guided Therapy community.

The workshop will concentrate on the computer science and engineering aspects of such systems, as the clinical aspects have been covered in previous NIH-related workshops. The agenda will include plenary talks that will review technical aspects of IGT as well as breakout sessions in which the participants will concentrate on issues raised by the talks.

Background on this workshop

The initial idea of this workshop was developed in ad-hoc meetings with collaborators across institutions including Georgetown, Johns Hopkins, UNC, NIH, GE Global Research, Kitware Inc., and Brigham and Women’s Hospital. The Program Committee welcomed and encouraged suggestions from the IGT community on the content of this workshop until mid July, 2006, when the program was finalized.

page-project-week.html.body:
PROJECT WEEK ACTIVITIES

PROJECT WEEK is a semi-annual event which draws 80-120 researchers. As of August 2014, it is a MICCAI endorsed event. The participants work collaboratively on open-science solutions for problems that lie on the interfaces of the fields of computer science, mechanical engineering, biomedical engineering, and medicine. In contrast to conventional conferences and workshops the primary focus of the Project Weeks is to make progress in projects (as opposed to reporting about progress). The objective of the Project Weeks is to provide a venue for this community of medical open source software creators. Project Weeks are open to all, are publicly advertised, and are funded through fees paid by the attendees. Participants are encouraged to stay for the entire event.

PROJECT WEEK ACTIVITIES. Everyone shows up with a project. Some people are working on the platform. Some people are developing algorithms. Some people are applying the tools to their research problems. We begin the week by introducing projects and connecting teams. We end the week by reporting progress. In addition to the ongoing working sessions, breakout sessions are organized ad-hoc on a variety of special topics. These topics include: discussions of software architecture, presentations of new features and approaches and topics such as Image Guided Therapy.

Several funded projects use the Project Week as a place to convene and collaborate. These include NAC, AT-NCIGT, T32 Multidisciplinary Training, QIICR, OCAIRO, SlicerIGT and OpenIGTLink.

page-prostate-core.html.body:
There are two complex issues that drive the clinical need to change current paradigms for prostate cancer (PCa): The inability to predict aggressiveness of a given cancer, which in turn leads to over treatment, and the increasing evidence that disease progression in men with seemingly low-risk PCa is due to inadequate biopsy sampling. Recent trends indicate that the treatment of patients with localized PCa is shifting more and more towards either active surveillance or focal therapy. Technical solutions to address these challenges, and their validation in clinic, are lacking. We are working to address these challenges by integrating innovative MR image acquisition and analysis with the MR targeted biopsy platform we developed in the previous cycle. We are developing a diagnostic biomedical imaging platform to detect, characterize and diagnose prostate cancer and will provide new opportunities to understand the aggressiveness and heterogeneity of prostate cancer and ultimately allow for development and testing of new predictive markers in focal therapy. Our projects are:

Platform for validating novel imaging biomarkers with molecular and routine pathology.  We are developing methods of assessment of tumor heterogeneity by supplementing mpMRI with new hypoxia and multi b value MR imaging and add molecular profiling to the pathology options for core biopsy tissue, thus provide a unique platform for imaging, biopsy and both routine and molecular pathology. We will correlate genomic diversity with MR imaging parameters. We will propose novel motion compensation techniques combined with hypoxia imaging that will be applied jointly with the multi-b-value diffusion weighted imaging (DWI) for improved characterization of PCa. These novel-imaging approaches will be validated in biopsy and cryotherapy patient cohorts. (Contact: Clare M. Tempany, Fiona Fennessy)

Platform for focal cryoablation of PCa with accurate temperature mapping and motion compensation. Our goal is to develop and evaluate thermometry methods to monitor MR-guided focal cryoablation for localized prostate cancer, by internal ice ball thermometry using a “voxelwise thermal history” method. We will develop and test a new method for tracking the prostate gland motion, using active MR tracking coils embedded in a urethral warming catheter, investigate Ultrashort TE (UTE) MRI to monitor the internal thermal dosimetry within the ice-ball, and develop and evaluate software for voxel-wise thermal history tracking during all stages of the procedure. (Contact: Junichi Tokuda)

Informatics solution in support of targeted prostate biopsy and focal therapy for localized prostate cancer. This aim will have three tasks: 1) develop software tools to support structured PCa reporting and image registration for biopsy and focal therapy applications; 2) investigate and implement improved practices for structured data collection and provenance, prepare and disseminate curated validation datasets to facilitate validation of the role of mpMRI in cancer characterization and the evaluation of image registration accuracy/reliability; 3) investigate methods for non-rigid registration to enable recovery of prostate gland deformation for treatment response assessment and propose and apply methodologies for statistical assessment of the reliability of the registration tools. All three projects are interconnected, and leverage unique resources provided by this Center. In addition to developing novel technologies, we are creating a platform for collecting validation imaging datasets annotated with the analysis results, molecular and pathology markers, to build a unique resource for investigating the role of imaging and development of novel image analysis tools for prostate cancer. (Contact: Andriy Fedorov)

Software and Documentation

3D Slicer, a comprehensive open source platform for medical image analysis, contains several modules that have been contributed by us for Image-Guided Prostate Interventions. These include:

  • BRAINSFitIGT: Image Registration for MR-Guided Prostate Biopsy
  • SliceTracker: 3D Slicer Extension for Tracking Prostate Motion during MR-guided Prostate Biopsies
  • N4ITKBiasFieldCorrection: MR Inhomogeneity Correction
  • MultiVolumeImporter: Importing Multi-Volume Datasets
  • PkModeling: Pharmacokinetic Modeling of DCE MRI Data using Tofts Model
  • MultiVolumeExplorer: Visualization and Exploration of Multi-Volume Data
  • MR-guided Prostate Interventions with 3D Slicer and the NA-MIC Kit

These presentations have been selected as tutorials for readers interested in learning about the clinical science and technology of the Prostate Core.

  • Preliminary Accuracy Evaluation of 3T MRI-guided Transperineal Prostate Biopsy with Grid Template. (Tokuda, ISMRM 2011)

page-prostate-image-reporting-and-data-s.body:
In recent years, multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) of the prostate has emerged a robust imaging approach for non-invasive characterization of prostate cancer at 3T (Hegde et al. 2013). mpMRI includes morphological (T2-weighted Imaging, or T2WI) and functional imaging (Diffusion Weighted Imaging with high b-values (>1600) (DWI), Dynamic Contrast Enhanced (DCE), and Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopic Imaging (MRSI) sequences). While the performance of the individual sequences is being investigated, and the acquisition techniques are being refined, integration of mpMRI into the clinical practice has been challenging due to the lack of consistent approaches for assessing mpMRI and reporting of the clinical findings. Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS) is a scoring system that aims to enable consistent interpretation, communication and reporting of prostate multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) findings (Barentsz et al. 2012; Dickinson et al. 2011). In 2015 version 2 of the PI-RADS guidelines were released by an international group of prostate imaging experts (Barentsz et al. 2015; Weinreb et al. 2016).

NCIGT Prostate project is actively involved in research projects that are related to the development and promotion of adoption of PI-RADS v2 along several directions:

  • All prostate MR exams at our BWH site are performed according to the PI-RADS v2 guidelines.
  • We are collecting clinical evidence in support of evaluation and refinement of PI-RADS (see recent studies by Hassanzadeh et al. (Hassanzadeh et al. 2016))
  • We are applying PI-RADS as part of the mpMRI evaluation protocol in the preparation and planning all stages of the in-bore MRI-guided prostate biopsy procedures, in place of the Likert scale rating used in the initial stages of the project described in (Penzkofer et al. 2015)
  • Facilitated by several collaborations, such as the one with the Quantitative Image Informatics for Cancer Research (QIICR) project, we are developing and improving DICOM standard to enable communication of image processing results, biopsy outcomes and PI-RADS scores.
  • We are developing infrastructure within 3D Slicer, our clinical research platform, to support PI-RADS reading workflows.

page-research.html.body:
Image Guided Therapy (IGT) is a foundational discipline that involves the integration of imaging into procedural medicine used in surgery, radiation oncology, and interventional radiology. The notion that IGT is more efficient, more effective, and less expensive than conventional surgery has been confirmed both in extensive long-term studies and in ongoing revolutionary applications in the operating room. We have laid critical groundwork with this extraordinary technology during the last two decades.

2015-2020

During this period our work was divided into four technology research and development (TRD) projects. The Prostate TRD developed novel platforms to allow for molecular profiling of prostate cancer and imaging to allow for improved predictive markers for guiding biopsy and focal therapy, and by use of image processing methods for monitoring treatment effect. The Neurosurgery TRD developed mass spectrometry as a biomarker for intraoperative surgical decision making to better define tumor extent. Advanced functional mapping using fMRI+DTI was used for individualized treatment planning. The Computation TRD developed specialized multimodal image registration algorithms and custom hardware for motion compensation to improve tumor localization and functional mapping. The Guidance TRD developed novel instrument and tumor tracking technologies to accurately deliver therapy despite significant physiological motion and tissue deformation.

2020-2025

Under the restructured Advanced Technologies–National Center for Image-Guided Therapy (AT-NCIGT), this cycle delivered quantifiable improvements in surgical and patient outcomes through detailed assessment of tissue architecture heterogeneity, deep-learning-based image registration, uniform data curation and annotation, and software and devices for intraprocedural guidance. Research was organized into three TRD projects. TRD 1, Imaging Cancer Heterogeneity, characterized tumors and their surroundings at macroscopic, microscopic, and molecular scales. TRD 2, Deep Learning, developed weakly-supervised deep learning methods for image-guided brain tumor surgery, lung surgery, and transperineal in-bore prostate biopsy, along with infrastructure for curating imaging data. TRD 3, Intraoperative Devices, delivered devices via 3D Slicer and OpenIGTLink, including intraoperative needle guidance for prostate biopsy, navigation for thoracoscopic lung surgery, and implantable microdevices for difficult-to-access tissues such as the brain.

2026-2030

Building on decades of technical and clinical leadership, the Center now enters its next cycle as the Advanced Technologies–National Center for Image-Guided Therapy (AT-NCIGT), continuing to lead advancements in image-guided approaches including MR-guided neurosurgery, prostate interventions, and focused ultrasound therapy. This renewal of our NIH P41 Center targets three critical needs in IGT and cancer therapy: high-fidelity MR imaging, in vivo deployment of image-guided microdevices (IMDs), and the development of enabling technologies, leveraging high-field MRI platforms alongside novel IMD systems and advanced enabling tools. For the period 2026-2030, our research is divided into three technology research and development (TRD) projects.

TRD 1 - Imaging Cancer Heterogeneity with High-Fidelity MRI

Imaging Cancer Heterogeneity with High-Fidelity MRI focuses on advanced quantitative MRI techniques — diffusion and chemical exchange saturation transfer (CEST) imaging — to support diagnosis, preoperative imaging, intervention guidance, and treatment monitoring, enabling robust, high-resolution, and reproducible imaging biomarkers.

LEARN MORE

TRD 2 - Multiscale Tumor Analysis

Multiscale Tumor Analysis for Personalized Therapy extends implantable microdevice (IMD) technology into a standardized platform for in situ drug response testing, pairing image-guided delivery and retrieval with a multi-omic tissue analysis pipeline to guide personalized treatment selection and predict drug resistance.

LEARN MORE

TRD 3 - Data-Driven Image-Guided Therapy

Enabling Technologies for Data-Driven Image-Guided Therapy develops data-driven, closed-loop systems for precision needle placement, augmented-reality-guided navigation for lymph node resection, and open software infrastructure — built on 3D Slicer and OpenIGTLink — to support dynamic, patient-specific image guidance.

LEARN MORE

MICCAI 2023 Workshop on Robotics, AI, and Imaging for Point of Care Surgical Guidance

October 8th, 2023

Submit Your Paper Call for Papers

We are pleased to announce the Workshop on Robotics, AI, and Imaging for Point of Care Surgical Guidance, to be held virtually as part of the MICCAI conference on October 8, 2023. The workshop is organized by Laura Brattain, Jayender Jagadeesan, and Tina Kapur, and the URL for the workshop is www.ncigt.org/RobsAI.

The workshop aims to bring together researchers, clinicians, and industry leaders to discuss recent advances and challenges in the development and translation of innovative technologies for point of care surgical guidance. We invite original contributions that address the following topics:

  • Integration of robotics, AI, and imaging for surgical guidance
  • Image-guided navigation and visualization for surgical interventions
  • Machine learning and deep learning for therapy guidance and decision support
  • Novel sensors and modalities for point of care guidance
  • Clinical translation and evaluation of point of care surgical guidance technologies

We welcome both theoretical and practical contributions, as well as papers that report on work in progress or describe novel approaches. All submissions will undergo a rigorous peer-review process by the program committee, and accepted papers will be published in the workshop proceedings as 8-page papers.

We look forward to your submissions and your participation in the workshop.

Best regards,

Laura Brattain, Jayender Jagadeesan, and Tina Kapur
Workshop Organizers

Submission Guidelines

Papers must be written in English and formatted according to the MICCAI 2023 guidelines. The maximum length of the paper is 10 pages (excluding references), and the submission should include an abstract of no more than 300 words. Papers should be submitted electronically through the workshop submission site CMT between May 15 and June 30, 2023.

Submit Your Paper Important Dates
  • Paper submissions open: May 15, 2023
  • Paper submission deadline: June 30, 2023
  • Notification of paper acceptance: July 30, 2023
  • Camera-ready paper deadline: August 15, 2023

page-software-and-tutorials.html.body:
We provide educational subject materials based on AT-NCIGT methodologies and clinical applications. Based on use-cases from Prostate Cancer, Neurosurgery, and other clinical applications relevant to our users, we develop subject matter for educating the next generation of IGT researchers.

The following is a collection of electronic resources provided by AT-NCIGT. This includes software, data, tutorials, presentations, and additional documentation.

SOFTWARE

  • 3D Slicer
  • OpenIGTLink
  • ROS for Medical Robotics (ROS-MED)
  • Fast Imaging Library

AFFILIATED SOFTWARE

TCIA Browser — a 3D Slicer extension for searching, previewing, and downloading imaging collections from The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA) directly into 3D Slicer.

Developed by QIICR as part of the TCIA Data Analysis Center.

TUTORIALS

  • User-made Video Playlists and Demos
  • AT-NCIGT Fast Imaging Library
  • SlicerIGT Tutorials
  • All Slicer Tutorials
  • AT-NCIGT Abdominal Intervention
  • Perk Tutor SlicerIGT Based Training Platform for Image-guided Interventions

DATA

  • Prostate MR Image Database
  • ReMIND: The Brain Resection Multimodal Imaging Database (TCIA)
  • Datasets and open-source software from the Surgical Navigation and Robotics Laboratory

MOVIES

  • Introducing the AT-NCIGT Team Work

page-training-in-image-guidance-precisio.body:
TRAINING IN IMAGE GUIDANCE, PRECISION DIAGNOSIS AND THERAPY T32 PROGRAM

The Training in Image Guidance, Precision Diagnosis and Therapy (IGT) T32 Program at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, led by Dr. Lauren O’Donnell and Dr. Fiona Fennessy, trains outstanding postdoctoral fellows at the intersection of medicine and technology.

Supported by the National Institutes of Health (T32EB025823), the program provides a highly interdisciplinary training environment spanning engineering, computer science, medical imaging, artificial intelligence, multiomics, surgical robotics, targeted therapeutics, and clinical research.

PROGRAM OVERVIEW

Image-guided therapy (IGT) plays a crucial role in modern medicine, providing a precise and personalized roadmap for interventions such as biopsy, ablation, surgery, deep brain stimulation, and radiation oncology. IGT brings together image guidance—including image acquisition, processing, and analysis—and precision diagnosis—including integration of data from multiple sources—to guide therapies across a broad range of clinical disciplines.

Our program prepares the next generation of MD and PhD investigators to advance this rapidly evolving field through integrated clinical and technical training.

The IGT T32 provides a two-year mentored postdoctoral research experience that combines cutting-edge technical research with exposure to clinical image-guided diagnosis and therapy. Each fellow receives complementary technical and clinical mentorship while participating in interdisciplinary research, educational activities, and career development designed to prepare for an independent career in biomedical research.

PROGRAM LEADERSHIP

Lauren O’Donnell, PhD
Program Co-Director

Fiona M. Fennessy, MD, PhD
Program Co-Director

Krisztina Fischer, MD, PhD, MMSc-Med Ed
Director of Education

ELIGIBILITY & FELLOWSHIP SUPPORT

The IGT T32 supports four postdoctoral fellowship positions in a two-year mentored research program.

Applicants must hold an MD, PhD, or equivalent doctoral degree and have a scientific or clinical background relevant to the program. PhD applicants are welcome from a broad range of scientific, engineering, and computational disciplines. MD applicants must have completed residency training and may come from specialties including diagnostic and interventional radiology, surgery, radiation oncology, pathology, and other areas relevant to image-guided therapy.

In accordance with NIH requirements, trainees must be U.S. citizens, noncitizen nationals, or permanent residents at the time of appointment.

Compensation is commensurate with qualifications and years of training, in accordance with BWH postdoctoral guidelines.

HOW TO APPLY

Applications are accepted on a rolling basis. Start dates are flexible depending on available trainee slots.

Applicants should submit the following materials via email:

  • Curriculum vitae (CV)
  • Personal statement describing short- and long-term career goals and how participation in the IGT T32 Program would support those goals
  • Research interests and potential mentor(s) selected from the program’s research themes
  • Names and contact information for three references; letters may be requested during the selection process
  • Confirmation of U.S. citizenship, noncitizen national, or permanent resident status

For questions or to submit application materials, please contact:

Lauren O’Donnell, PhD
Program Co-Director
Associate Professor of Radiology, Harvard Medical School
odonnell@bwh.harvard.edu

SELECTION

Applications are reviewed based on academic and research accomplishments, potential for career development, alignment with the program’s research and training themes, and potential to benefit from interdisciplinary clinical and technical mentorship. Selected applicants will be invited to interview.

FACULTY MENTORS & RESEARCH THEMES

Fellows are matched with faculty mentors based on their research interests and career goals, with interdisciplinary mentorship designed to provide complementary technical and clinical perspectives. Faculty span the BWH Departments of Radiology, Neurosurgery, Pathology, Psychiatry, and Neurology, providing opportunities for research across a broad range of clinical disciplines.

1. MULTIOMICS FOR IGT: RADIOMICS, PATHOMICS, METABOLOMICS

Faculty: Fiona Fennessy, MD, PhD | Sabina Signoretti, MD | Alexander Lin, PhD

This theme explores how imaging can be integrated with pathology, genomics, spectroscopy, and metabolomics to better characterize tumor heterogeneity and guide precision diagnosis and treatment. Fellows gain exposure to diagnostic and interventional radiology, pathology, and computational approaches for integrating multiomic data into clinically meaningful models.

2. ADVANCED MR AND COMPUTATIONAL IMAGE SCIENCE

Faculty: Lauren O’Donnell, PhD | Yogesh Rathi, PhD | Yanmei Tie, PhD | Daniel Paech, MD, PhD | Carl-Fredrik Westin, PhD

This theme combines state-of-the-art MRI with advanced computational methods for studying brain structure, function, and disease. Research opportunities include 7T and high-resolution MRI, diffusion and microstructure imaging, MR spectroscopy, brain mapping, deep learning, image-guided interventions, and open-source software development using platforms such as 3D Slicer and SlicerDMRI.

3. MICRODEVICES AND SURGICAL ROBOTICS

Faculty: Oliver Jonas, PhD | Nobuhiko Hata, PhD | Jayender Jagadeesan, PhD | Ron Kikinis, MD | Junichi Tokuda, PhD

This theme focuses on developing novel devices and robotic technologies for image-guided diagnosis and therapy. Projects span drug-releasing intratumoral microdevices, robotic catheters and scopes, shape-sensing needles, and image-guided systems for minimally invasive procedures, with strong opportunities for clinical translation and collaboration with industry.

4. TARGETED BRAIN THERAPEUTICS

Faculty: Nathan McDannold, PhD | Nicholas Todd, PhD | Michael Fox, MD, PhD

This theme brings together imaging, neuroscience, and therapeutic technology to develop and improve treatments that target brain circuits. Fellows can pursue research in MRI-guided focused ultrasound, deep brain stimulation, neuromodulation, and network-based approaches to treating neurological and psychiatric disorders within a highly interdisciplinary clinical and research environment.

5. MACHINE LEARNING FOR ROBUST SENSING AND IMAGING

Faculty: Sarah Frisken, PhD | Alexandra Golby, MD | Bruno Madore, PhD | Tina Kapur, PhD

This theme develops machine-learning methods that combine medical images with real-time imaging and sensor data to improve image-guided procedures. Projects include intraoperative tumor segmentation, image registration for neuronavigation, surgical tool tracking, multimodal imaging, and ML-enhanced image acquisition, with opportunities for both algorithm development and clinical application.

6. CROSS-SCALE BIOMARKER INTEGRATION

Faculty: Nathalie Agar, PhD | Sandro Santagata, MD, PhD

This theme integrates information across molecular, cellular, microscopic, and macroscopic scales to better characterize disease and guide precision treatment. Fellows can work with emerging technologies including mass spectrometry imaging, spatial metabolomics, single-cell RNA sequencing, multiplexed tissue imaging, and computational approaches for relating molecular biomarkers to imaging and clinical information.

TRAINING EXPERIENCE

Each fellow receives interdisciplinary co-mentorship, with a primary mentor overseeing day-to-day research and training and a secondary mentor providing complementary expertise, regular feedback, and a broader clinical or technical perspective.

Training is tailored to each fellow’s research interests and career goals, with fellows identifying thematic areas and mentors during the interview and selection process. The curriculum evolves as new technologies emerge and are translated into clinical practice.

The training experience includes six core components:

  • Interdisciplinary mentorship from complementary technical and clinical faculty
  • A mentored research project aligned with the fellow’s scientific and career goals
  • Hands-on experience in image-guided therapy and exposure to clinical IGT environments
  • Personalized education and career development
  • Scientific communication and grant-writing training
  • Multidisciplinary training and community engagement, including the T32 seminar series and program events

page-trd-1-imaging-cancer-heterogeneity..body:
TR&D 1 Team: Stephan E. Maier, MD, PhD (Project Lead) • Daniel Paech, MD, PhD • Carl-Fredrik Westin, PhD

Led by STEPHAN MAIER, the focus areas of the IMAGING CANCER HETEROGENEITY WITH HIGH-FIDELITY MRI TRD are:

  • Developing a motion-compensated, multi-shot, multi-echo 3D diffusion imaging sequence for unprecedented isotropic high-resolution imaging with improved spatial fidelity, on a high-performance head-only 3T MRI system.
  • Establishing a robust fitting framework for reproducible apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) measurements that eliminate protocol- and scanner-position dependence for consistent, multi-site comparable imaging biomarkers.
  • Building a harmonization framework — using temperature-stabilized phantoms, vendor-neutral Pulseq sequences, and automated optimization — to detect and correct scanner-induced bias in chemical exchange saturation transfer (CEST) MRI.
page-trd-1-imaging-cancer-heterogeneity..title: TR&D 1 – Imaging Cancer Heterogeneity

page-trd-2-deep-learning.html.body:
TR&D 2 Team: Oliver Jonas, PhD (Project Lead) • Sharath Bhagavatula, MD • Nobuhiko Hata, PhD

Led by OLIVER JONAS, the focus areas of the MULTISCALE TUMOR ANALYSIS TRD are:

  • Extending the implantable microdevice (IMD) platform’s technical functionality to support image-guided delivery and non-surgical retrieval across diverse anatomical sites.
  • Developing an integrated multi-omic tissue analysis pipeline for scalable, high-resolution pathological characterization of IMD drug responses.
  • Building and applying a clinical correlation framework to validate IMD-based biomarkers for predicting drug resistance and treatment response.
page-trd-2-deep-learning.html.title: TR&D 2 – Deep Learning

page-trd-3-intraoperative-devices.html.body:
TR&D 3 Team: Junichi Tokuda, PhD (Project Lead) • Jayender Jagadeesan, PhD • Nobuhiko Hata, PhD

Led by JUNICHI TOKUDA, the focus areas of the DATA-DRIVEN IMAGE-GUIDED THERAPY TRD are:

  • Data-driven, closed-loop systems for precision needle placement, using patient-specific biomechanical “digital twin” models to compensate for organ motion during percutaneous prostate interventions.
  • Augmented reality (AR)-guided navigation tools for lymph node resection, using SLAM-based surface reconstruction to localize PET-avid nodes and compensate for tissue deformation during bladder cancer staging.
  • Open software infrastructure, integrated with 3D Slicer, to disseminate data-driven image guidance tools — including digital twin modeling, surface reconstruction, and robotic control — for a wide range of clinical applications.

page-video-assisted-thoracoscopic-surger.body:
In the AMIGO suite, we have developed a new surgical approach for treatment of small lung nodules, lesions that are not obviously malignant, but could harbor early lung cancer. If surgical resection is warranted, these lesions are often difficult to palpate, necessitating a large resection of lung tissue to ensure that the lesion is completely removed. Our protocol utilizes the intraoperative fluoroscopy and C-arm CT capability of the AMIGO suite to place image-guided fiducials around these small lung lesions and improve the precision in localizing the lesions. The protocol has enabled our precise targeting of lung tumors and minimizing the extent to which normal lung tissue is resected while achieving adequate surgical margins. With the recently developed guidelines for screening smokers with low-dose CT, many more small lung nodules are expected to be detected. The successful development of our surgical approach using the AMIGO suite could prove highly beneficial to patients with these lesions.

Image-guided targeting of lesions for surgical resection is not a new concept. However, many current techniques are without the benefit of fiducial placement with intraoperative fluoro-CT, relying, instead, on preoperative image guidance or on intraoperative ultrasound guidance. These techniques are associated with the risk of complications and the limitations of image resolution. Our surgical approach in AMIGO utilizes C-arm CT image guidance in a controlled operating room setting. It is designed to maximize patient safety while using C-arm CT imaging to target small lung lesions so that pathologic lung tissue may be completely excised while preserving as much normal lung tissue as possible.

Lung cancer remains the deadliest malignancy. The National Lung Cancer Screening Trial found that screening smokers who fit the criteria using low-dose CT has a significant impact on reducing mortality. The screening detects with precision many small lung lesions and our new surgical approach has demonstrated safe and effective preliminary results for excising these lesions with precision. We plan to continue evaluating the long-term outcomes so that our surgical approach can be translated for use in other clinical settings. Hybrid operating rooms like the AMIGO suite are becoming more prevalent. In clinical setting without this technology, our surgical approach may be adapted for use with preoperative CT image guidance to place the fiducials marking the small lung lesion.

This case study below illustrates the iVATS workflow in AMIGO. A 20-year-old male was diagnosed with a small lesion in the right lower lobe of the lung. Preoperative PET-CT showed a 9 x 7 mm lung nodule that was also visible on PET imaging. Localizing such a small lesion by finger palpation intraoperatively is almost impossible, and so an entire lobe of a 20-year-old patient would have had to be removed. The patient underwent an iVATS procedure in AMIGO. Using the techniques we developed, we were able to accurately localize the lesion intraoperatively under C-arm CT guidance using two imaging fiducials called T-bars. Thereafter, using these two fiducials as surrogate markers for the tumor, the surgeon identified the lesion and performed a wedge resection surgery. Pathology results confirmed that the lesion was a carcinoid and the margins were negative.
